newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac set for big gamble with early French poll.
newsitem.headline: Chirac set for big gamble with early French poll.

text.p: Jacques Chirac seems set to take the biggest gamble of his presidency by calling a snap general election in hopes of securing his parliamentary majority by separating the French and European calendars.
Political sources say Chirac will broadcast to the nation on Monday to announce a dissolution of parliament and an election, probably in the first week of June, after a short campaign.

Victory would give him a working centre-right majority for the rest of his seven-year term until 2002 and free his hands to take whatever further austerity measures are necessary to ensure France qualifies for a single European currency.
Yet defeat would reduce the Gaullist president to a virtual lame duck forced to share power with a hostile Socialist-led government.

Neither the president nor Prime Minister Alain Juppe seem popular enough in opinion polls to suggest this is a safe bet. Both have negative approval ratings, with support for Juppe down below 30 percent in most surveys.
"This is very risky. If the right were defeated, Chirac's presidential legitimacy would be seriously holed," said analyst Roland Cayrol, head of the CSA polling institute.
So why would Chirac take that risk when his coalition controls 478 of the 577 seats in the National Assembly and the next election was not due until March 1998?

The answer, according to most pundits, is that he needs to take harsher austerity measures to bring down public sector deficits and qualify France for European monetary union in 1999, so he needs to get the election out of the way first.

He may also have concluded that the economy is unlikely to revive sufficiently by early 1998 to bring down record 12.8 percent unemployment or give voters the feeling they have more money in their pockets.

"The coalition is bound to lose a substantial number of seats since it controls four-fifths of the outgoing Assembly. This is an orderly retreat, programmed to enable the coalition to win nine months early," said Jerome Jaffre, political director of the SOFRES polling firm.

Allowing the electoral calendar to run its course could lead to an even more risky collision with the timetable for a single currency. The first countries to qualify for EU monetary union are due to be selected in late April or early May next year.

The Gaullist nightmare is an election campaign waged against a background of strikes and demonstrations over austerity measures imposed in the name of Europe. That would reopen divisions over the single currency which have healed only superficially since a 1992 referendum on the Maastricht treaty.
Another factor in Chirac's calculation may be that the left-wing opposition looks invitingly weak.

The Socialists, still convalescing from a landslide 1993 general election defeat, have recently been embarrassed by a scandal over the late president Francois Mitterrand's illegal bugging of lawyers, journalists and politicians.

Socialist leader Lionel Jospin, who scored a creditable 47.3 percent in the 1995 presidential election against Chirac, has also appeared out of phase with public opinion and grassroots party activists over immigration and the fight against Jean-Marie Le Pen's extreme-right National Front.
The Left is split over the single currency, with the anti-EMU Communists demanding a referendum.
Chirac may also reckon that the longer he continues with present policy, the more mainstream conservative voters will switch to the National Front.

Even though the polls show the Left and Right almost level, analysts say well-entrenched incumbents tend to enjoy a premium in most French elections, and the coalition has four times more incumbents than the left.
So how much of a risk would Chirac be taking?

The main threat is that an early poll could unleash a wave of voter discontent over his broken 1995 presidential election pledges to bring down unemployment, cut taxes and raise wages, especially if Jospin ran a better-than-expected campaign.
Pollsters say that is a real risk, but the president appears to be convinced it is a smaller risk than allowing the electoral calendar to take its course.
